case_studies.title: LiveLoRA: Exact KV Cache Migration Across LoRA Updates for LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.
case_studies.summary: LiveLora lets you upgrade an LLM adapter without re-running the whole chat history, saving time and storage. It freezes early decoder layers and keeps KV cache entries consistent across adapter updates, giving almost 69× speedups over full-history re-prefill on large sessions.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM-serving, update your deployment pipeline to keep the first decoder blocks frozen and enable LiveLora’s cache migration logic: 1) Freeze lower blocks and adapter down-projections. 2) During a new adapter release, migrate existing KV cache entries to the new format and recompute the final token. 3) Commit the updated cache and logits before serving next token. This reduces re‑prefill costs and storage for long-running sessions.
case_studies.score_reasoning: LiveLoRA offers a concrete, low-overhead technique to migrate KV caches across LoRA updates, directly benefiting LLM agent deployment pipelines and reducing operational costs for IT engineers managing large session fleets. The method is grounded in a provable equivalence and demonstrates significant speedups, indicating practical applicability. However, the paper does not appear to provide released code or a ready-to-deploy system, so while the idea is mature, it remains somewhat theoretical at this stage. Nonetheless, an engineer could implement the approach or offer it as a service within a short timeframe, giving it a solid monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning
case_studies.abstract: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to 5.8\% at 4K and from 41.8\% to 6.5\% at 8K. At 4K, generation is 2.05$\times$ faster for 4B and 2.23$\times$ faster for 8B than unforced 8K decoding in local amortized batch time. Tail-CRC thus enables reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning from a single rollout.
case_studies.summary: Hard token limits stop LLMs before answering, risking wrong outputs. The authors built Tail-CRC, a single‑rollout method that first trains a solver to respect token budgets, then uses conformal risk control to decide whether to submit the answer. It boosts correct‑submission rates by 15–30 points, cuts wrong answers to under 7%, and saves 4–13% inference cost.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference with token budgets, use Tail‑CRC: 1) fine‑tune your model to stop at the budget with a binary reward; 2) freeze the model and add a conformal risk‑control layer that checks token‑log‑probability surprise; 3) deploy the single‑rollout pipeline and tune the risk target to keep wrong‑submission rates below your desired threshold.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a method (Tail-CRC) that directly improves LLM deployment efficiency and error control—critical for engineers working with large language models in production. It proposes a concrete, single‑rollout approach that could be integrated into existing LLM inference pipelines, offering tangible performance gains and cost savings. However, the work is still at a research prototype stage; there is no evidence of released code, public deployments, or a fully tested system, which limits maturity. Despite this, the technique is actionable enough for engineers to experiment with and could be turned into a commercial or internal service within a short timeframe, hence a moderate monetisation score. Overall, the paper scores well on real‑world impact and monetisation potential, but lower on maturity, giving a total of 45. No low signal flag.

case_studies.title: TideSand: Performance-Accurate Sandbox Multiplexing for LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: We propose TideSand, a sandbox system that intelligently multiplexes resources for performance-sensitive LLM agents, such as auto research agents working on system measurement tasks. TideSand combines three key ideas: agent-aware scheduling, which schedules sandbox execution intelligently at the tool call level to avoid resource contention; speculative swapping, which offloads the memory of sandboxes waiting on inference and restores it before their next tool call; and selective rollback, which checkpoints selected sandboxes when contention occurs and restores them when machines are idle. We evaluate TideSand across six model-workload pairs on AlgoTune, Terminal-Bench 4.0, and Terminal-Bench Science. TideSand achieves 3.8-10x higher throughput than strict reservation while maintaining tool-call fidelity, or 7-44% higher fidelity than overcommit baselines at similar throughput. Moreover, TideSand reduces the evaluation error on Algotune by 19x through improved tool-call fidelity. We hope the work motivates future research to maintain tool call fidelity while keeping resource utilization high through statistical multiplexing.
case_studies.summary: TideSand is a sandbox system that smartly shares CPU and memory across multiple large‑language‑model agents. It schedules tool calls, swaps out idle memory, and rolls back only when needed, giving up to 10× more throughput and up to 44% better call accuracy compared with simple reservation or overcommit approaches.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) evaluate whether your LLM workloads hit CPU or memory contention; 2) if so, test TideSand’s agent‑aware scheduling and speculative swapping on a small set of models; 3) integrate the sandbox layer before deploying agents to improve throughput and reliability.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses resource management for LLM agents, which could benefit IT engineers deploying large models on shared infrastructure. It demonstrates performance gains over benchmarks, indicating a working prototype, but lacks evidence of production deployment or released code, hence moderate maturity. The concepts could be monetised as a service to optimise LLM hosting, but require further engineering to be ready for commercial use. Overall impact is moderate, maturity low, monetisation potential moderate, leading to a total score above the 30 threshold.

case_studies.title: TowerBridge: Bridging the Dual-Encoder Modality Gap via Weight-Space Programming
case_studies.abstract: CLIP-style dual encoders map images and text through two separate towers into a shared embedding space, where the two modalities occupy distinct regions separated by a modality gap. Retrieval fails when wrong matches, or hard negatives, outrank the correct one, and the gap is the usual suspect. Yet removing it post hoc degrades retrieval on every CLIP checkpoint we test. We introduce a paired statistic that identifies directions where the two towers agree more on hard negatives than on matched pairs. Mildly attenuating these directions improves retrieval while largely preserving the gap. We arrive at this correction through weight-space programming: guided by the statistic, an LLM agent inspects both towers and writes closed-form weight edits without backpropagation. Free to edit any component, the agent improves COCO test retrieval on all 13 CLIP checkpoints and edits an output projection in 12 of the 13. We distill and refine its recurring correction into TowerBridge, a closed-form recipe motivated by a first-order analysis of the hard-negative margin. Computed in seconds from 25,000 labelled pairs, it requires no model-specific tuning and leaves the architecture and inference cost unchanged. TowerBridge improves COCO test retrieval by 16.8 RSUM and Flickr30k test retrieval by 6.6 on average across all 21 evaluated CLIP checkpoints, including 8 unseen by the agent, while limiting any drop in ImageNet zero-shot accuracy to 0.5 points. It also reduces hubness on all 21 checkpoints and improves retrieval on 4 of 5 dual encoders from other families.
case_studies.summary: The paper solves the problem of a modality gap that hurts image‑text retrieval in CLIP‑style models. Researchers built TowerBridge, a quick, model‑agnostic recipe that tweaks weights based on a statistic to close the gap without hurting performance. It improves retrieval scores by up to 17 points on COCO and 6.6 on Flickr30k across many checkpoints, while keeping inference costs the same.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage dual‑encoder models, use TowerBridge: step 1 – run the provided script on 25,000 labelled pairs to compute the statistic; step 2 – apply the closed‑form weight edits to your encoder weights; step 3 – test retrieval and hubness – you should see a boost without extra inference cost.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on improving multimodal retrieval performance via weight-space programming on CLIP models, a niche research area with limited direct applicability to everyday IT infrastructure tasks. The method is presented as a closed-form recipe and is theoretically sound, but no evidence of released code or production deployment is provided, indicating moderate maturity. The technique offers only incremental improvements to retrieval metrics and lacks clear, immediate commercial or operational value for IT engineers managing cloud services, identity, or security, resulting in low monetisation potential. Overall, its relevance to the target audience is modest, yielding a total score below 30.
